query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that employs a machine‐learning framework trained on transferable features from binary alloy systems can accurately identify high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) with exceptionally low phonon thermal conductivity by effectively capturing the local chemical fluctuations and force-constant variations that enhance phonon scattering.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, entropy‐stabilized high‐entropy alloys (e.g., alloys similar to FeCoCrMnNi) with inherent lattice distortions and random atomic environments.
generation.intervention: Apply the predictive approach using an ML model with a transformation module that converts raw compositional and structural features from binary alloy datasets into an expanded feature space adaptable to HEAs.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted at room temperature and moderately low temperatures under standard thermal-insulation test conditions; samples should be synthesized to ensure a predominantly single-phase structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical fluctuations and force-constant fluctuations caused by severe lattice distortion mediate the increased phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: The approach works by quantifying how the random atomic environments in HEAs lead to enhanced force-constant fluctuations. These fluctuations scatter acoustic phonons more effectively than in more ordered materials, thus reducing phonon thermal conductivity. The ML model captures this relationship better than traditional theoretical models by learning latent correlations from binary systems.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict HEAs with lower phonon thermal conductivity (relative to baselines from conventional Callaway-Debye or similar models) with an improved accuracy margin—potentially showing around a 20% reduction in prediction error. Experimental samples identified by the model should exhibit reduced lattice thermal conductivity owing to stronger phonon scattering.
generation.baseline: Current predictive models (e.g., those based on simplified theoretical approaches) that do not fully incorporate the effects of local chemical disorder and force-constant fluctuations, leading to less accurate predictions of phonon thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to HEAs that maintain a uniform single-phase structure with high entropy; it may not extend to multiphase or compositionally segregated materials where additional scattering mechanisms or phase boundaries dominate the thermal transport.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement (e.g., the precise percentage reduction in prediction error) is uncertain due to variability in alloy compositions and experimental conditions; furthermore, the effectiveness of the feature transformation module when extrapolating from binary to multi-element systems remains to be fully validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a series of HEA compositions that are predicted by the model to have low phonon thermal conductivity. Synthesize these alloys under controlled conditions ensuring a single-phase structure. Measure their acoustic phonon dispersions and lattice thermal conductivity using techniques such as inelastic neutron scattering or time-domain thermoreflectance. Compare the experimental lattice thermal conductivity values with the model predictions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If for at least 70% of the tested HEA samples the experimentally measured lattice thermal conductivity deviates from the predicted values by more than ±10% (or if the model fails to correctly forecast the trend of lower conductivity relative to alloys predicted by conventional models), then the predictive approach is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This work shed light on the effect of constituent elements on local chemical fluctuation and lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy thermoelectric materials and also revealed the direct relationship between the fluctuation and atomic characteristic of elements, which could serve as a guide for tailoring local chemical fluctuation in the community of high-entropy materials.

Recently, entropy engineering has been used as a novel strategy to optimize the electrical and thermal transport properties of TE materials. By increasing element species, the mixing entropy in a material system increases quickly, and high-entropy materials with over five principal elements will be formed. Severe lattice distortion is usually the core phenomenon of high-entropy material—such distortion leads to strong scattering for heat-carrying phonons and results in low lattice thermal conductivity. Stabilizing single-phase structures by increasing entropy weakens the phase-boundary electron scattering in multiphase high-entropy material, thus providing a beneficial contribution to improve electrical transport properties, i.e., entropy-driven structural stabilization,. Therefore, the high-entropy-stabilized composition should work as a good matrix for further optimization of TE performance by integrating the traditional optimization strategy.

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. If this is unexpected from Mu’s theory, which would predict increased force-constant fluctuations due to the larger variability of random environments of a given atomic pair, it explains recent experimental reports on comparable phonon lattice thermal conductivities in our HEA and FeNi
